## Course Description

The emergence of intelligence and behavior from the complex interactions within the brain remains one of the most significant and unsolved mysteries in modern science. This is an exciting era. In the last decade, we have witnessed rapid advancements in experimental tools that now enable us to monitor and manipulate brain circuits with unprecedented precision. However, it is also a perplexing time. Neuroscientists are navigating the intricate landscapes of brain structures and dynamics. Mathematical theory has become crucial for integrating seemingly unrelated evidence, providing new insights, guiding new experiments, and identifying concepts and principles of brain function.

In this course, we will explore how physics, engineering, and mathematics have shaped our understanding of the brain. In particular, we will investigate the relationship between structure, dynamics, representation, and behavior. Special topics may include wiring optimization in neural circuit, attractor and chaotic dynamics in neural network, sensory and motor representation, biological learning rules, Hopfield network, and hierarchical control of behaviors. We will also discuss connections with modern machine learning methods. 


## Topics

Computational neuroscience originated from the attempt to apply mathematics and physics in neuroscience. Researchers
believe that such conjucture will offer us more insights into how brain works. These mathematical and physical tools
are similar to what we meet in some branches of artificial intelligence, which to some degrees shows their affinity. 

It is necessary to clarify that we do not plan to offer a comprehensive map of how brain works or how intelligence
emerges. It goes beyond our time and capability. Besides, we will not dip into the fundamental mechanics which preserves basic physiological activities. They are reserved to other courses, i.e., biophysics. We will narrow down
to a collection of works from 1900s to 2020s, and to its main part, from 1952 to 1997. Compared with some rigorious physics courses, it is more like a gallery. Party haven't been over in neuroscience. 

In this course, we will consider these topics in order, if time is allowed,

- Neuromorpholohy: we can explain the morphology of general neuronal elements, i.e., spines, dendrites, etc., via a
normative pathway. 
In this part you will find the direct connection between computational neuroscience and physics. 

- Single Neuron Behavior: We will introduce Hodgekin-Hulxuly model which is published in series of papers in 1952, and provide a biologically plausible model.
This part has relative independence in this course. Some comments claim that it gives little help to an understanding
of population activity. But the variants in dynamics is significant sometimes, and may offer new insights, i.e., BTSP.

- From Single to Multi-Neuron Behavior: Compared with cellular perspective and self-consistent network perspective, 
this part provides a interface, focusing on encoding and decoding information in neural system. 
We will meet plenty of statistics and information theory in this part, but it gives us something testable. Anyway,
math for neuroscience sake. 

- Multi Neuron Behavior: In this part, we will introduce so-called neural network, and it is also the most relative
part compared with field of artificial intelliegnce of 2010s. However, large language model has decisively changed
our life and the domain of AI. Computational neuroscience is the castle of connectivilism, but the latter will never
stay in its castle. 

For deeper and more frontier topics in computational neuroscience, there is a course for graduate student in the 
spring. If you are interested in other topics, welcome to the lab and journal club 4pm every Friday afternoon. 


## Prerequisites

Mathematical tools are required in each part, while physics is mostly in part one and two. Here is the list. 

- Part 1: some physics mindset
- Part 2: ODE
- Part 3: statistics, probability theory, linear algebra, information theory
- Part 4: statistical physics, machine learning

*Tip: Please do not try to master all of them. Collaboration is profound in this course.* 


## Grading

| Component | Weight |

If a solution with novelty or about a question tagged bonus, you can get a bonus.
Posting good question or offering good answer on the issue page will also receive a bonus. 

**Score** = 70% × (average homework) + 30% × (final exam) + bonus

*Tip: Although we have not met such scene, please do not abuse GitHub issue page for bonus. Explanation preserved by TA.*


## Recommended Textbooks

- Abbott &amp; Dayan, *Theoretical Neuroscience: Computational and Mathematical Modeling of Neural Systems* — [MIT Press](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262041997/theoretical-neuroscience/)
- Xiao-Jing Wang, *Theoretical Neuroscience: Understanding Cognition* — [Taylor &amp; Francis](https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/mono/10.1201/9781003459361/theoretical-neuroscience-xiao-jing-wang)
- Sterling &amp; Laughlin, *Principles of Neural Design* — [MIT Press](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262534680/principles-of-neural-design/)
- Grace Lindsay, *Models of the Mind: How Physics, Engineering and Mathematics Have Shaped Our Understanding of the Brain* — [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/Models-Mind-Engineering-Mathematics-Understanding/dp/1472966430)

*Tip: You don't have to read them all.
Reducing redundant information is another important capability in this course.*

## Policies

- **Late homework:** Homework submitted after the deadline will incur a penalty of **2 points per day**, unless you have emailed the TA in advance to arrange an extension.

- **Collaboration:** Collaboration is allowed, but you must state it in your submission, cite all sources properly, and clearly declare any use of AI tools. In this era, we will unavoidably collaborate with AI tools, and sometimes feel
overwhelmed or [*discouraged*](https://e.vnexpress.net/news/news/education/china-s-1st-female-fields-medalist-felt-discouraged-at-university-sparking-education-system-debate-5108204.html). Thus, as a researcher, you should try to preserve your *subjectivity*.

> ...if the authors cannot convincingly demonstrate that they can give a clear, expert-level talk on their results, that is correct and properly attributed, then the result should not be published.

— Terence Tao, the commentary of the [Leiden Declaration](https://leidendeclaration.ai/) on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics, in "[Mathematics in the Age of AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16753)", ICM 2026
